A while back, I had coffee with a CEO that was doing well selling into enterprises and mid-market companies. His product was very technical but easy to use, so his sales team could do demos remotely and without much help from engineering or solution architects. He wanted to go more enterprise. To sell bigger deals, he’d need more people on his team:
More engineers to handle complex integrations and security requirements
More pre-sales resources (solution consultants, presales eng) to assist prospects through longer sales cycles
Salespeople who understand how to navigate large procurement processes
This would double or triple his company size overnight. And he knew it wasn’t going to be simple. “It’s not just about having better products,” he said. “When you’re going upmarket, you have to become a different kind of company.”
What makes this particularly interesting is that this founder has been there before—his previous startup went public at $1B+ ARR, got acquired by Cisco for $2.6 billion, and then started again after the acquisition fell apart. He knows what it takes to build an enterprise-grade organization.
But here’s where things get really telling:
“I’m hesitant because once you start down this path, it’s hard to turn around. You can’t say ‘oh we don’t want to be an enterprise company anymore.’ Once you make those investments, they’re sunk costs whether you see them pay off or not.”
He’s worried about getting too big, even though he’s already built two successful tech companies. Why Enterprise Companies Are Willing to Buy From Small Vendors
So why would any CIO trust an eight-person company over a hundred-person one? The answer lies in understanding something counterintuitive about enterprise software purchasing decisions.

Their CAC efficiency metrics have improved dramatically.
This isn’t just good news for their business model—it signals they’re getting better at identifying which prospects convert and scaling the playbook accordingly.

answer:
So I was recently asked for some thoughts on how to stand out at an interview. It’s not that hard — just do your research and be honest. But many folks are struggling these days, so maybe it’s time to update my list:
Know every single thing you can about the company before the interview
. This is #1 because almost no one does this well enough. Go through their social media. Read all their recent press releases. Research their competition. Know who their top competitors are, what they look like, etc. There’s zero reason you shouldn’t know more than the CEO here. Be ready to talk to anyone, including the janitor or maintenance guy
. They might end up being your boss someday. Even if they aren’t now. Bring references ahead of time, but also have people they don’t expect
. Everyone knows how to bring 2-3 great LinkedIn recommendations. That’s easy. The best candidates will also find someone good that isn’t on LinkedIn, e.g., a VP at a prior company where they were successful. Or even better — the CEO themselves. Don’t hide anything
. If you got fired from your last job? Own it. Why did you get fired? What would you do differently today? Etc. Just own it. And don’t make excuses. In fact, as long as you’re honest, most founders will give you points for owning your mistakes. Show up early
. If nothing else, show respect by showing up 10 minutes early. And dress up
. Yes, everyone dresses casually these days. No matter what, dress business casual. Better yet, dress up. Show respect. Share what you’ve done and learned (and love) in your current role
. Make sure it’s relevant, however, to the new role. Do not simply read off your resume.

So I’ve been doing VC for over a decade now — and while things have changed since the peak of late 2020-early 2021, one thing has stayed constant:
VCs are worried
.
They worry when times are great because they think it’s all too good to be true (and sometimes it is), and they worry even more when things get harder.  The best ones just keep going, no matter what.  But everyone worries, especially if their latest check hasn’t had time to mature yet.
And right now, public multiples are worrisome indeed:
The median public B2B company trades at less than 5x ARR — the lowest multiple we’ve seen in decades
. Even growth companies are trading at barely double-digit multiples, down from nearly 30x in early 2021. This isn’t a cyclical correction; this is structural change. And yes, that will impact private valuations, too. If you’re not raising capital anytime soon, probably don’t sweat it much
. The reality is most startups outside of AI aren’t seeing any material impact on fundraising today. What matters is whether your investors believe you’ll compound fast enough to justify current prices. If you can demonstrate strong unit economics and clear paths to profitability or hypergrowth, you might actually benefit from lower expectations around exit timelines. But if you’re relying heavily on high-growth assumptions to raise rounds, you need to adjust those plans quickly. That doesn’t mean you should panic.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: How do you deal with a CFO that is very polished, well-spoken and has all his or her numbers right … when he/she misses burn rate projections almost every month?
I’ve been there many times.
First — let me tell you this isn’t really the CFO’s fault. Not entirely at least. The reason why your CFO may be missing the mark is likely due to one or more of the following reasons:
1/ They Don’t Know Your Business Well Enough Yet
CFOs aren’t always as “hands-on” as founders expect them to be. If they’re coming from a larger company or a different industry, they might not have deep enough understanding of your business model, customer segments, and sales cycles yet. This lack of contextual knowledge can lead to forecasting errors that compound over time.  This is common if a new hire comes from an environment where financial planning was outsourced or done by external partners rather than internal teams.
2/ Inadequate Data Quality & Systems Integration
If your accounting systems aren’t properly integrated with your CRM or other operational tools, it creates a data silo effect that prevents accurate forecasts. Or worse, the data is just plain inaccurate (see point #5). A good CFO should help identify these issues and implement solutions.
3/ Insufficient Customer Segmentation
Are they treating all customers equally for forecasting purposes? That’s usually wrong. You need to forecast revenue based on ACV tiers, growth rates, churn probabilities, etc. If they’re not doing this segmentation, their models will naturally underestimate future revenue potential.

No.
I know you want to move fast. You’ve probably been sold on the idea that AI is going to disrupt traditional sales and marketing playbooks overnight, especially with all the hype around LLMs and generative tools. And it’s true — AI can do some things at scale that humans just can’t match.
But here’s what most founders get wrong:
You need to build your human-first foundation before you layer AI on top of it. Not after.
Why This Order Matters More Than You Think
Here’s what happens when you flip this around: You deploy an AI SDR without proper human processes first, and then…
Your AI spams prospects with generic messaging they’d never respond to
Your AI books meetings for reps who aren’t ready or trained properly
Your AI creates more noise than actual pipeline because nobody’s segmenting correctly
Your AI burns through budget because nobody set clear ROI metrics upfront
Your AI becomes a shiny object that distracts from fixing broken human systems underneath
The biggest risk isn’t that your AI will fail (though it might). The bigger risk is that you’ll optimize for AI efficiency while optimizing nothing else. Your results will look impressive until they don’t — and by then, you’re deep into a hole trying to fix both problems simultaneously.

Before any AI agent touches your prospect list, make sure these fundamentals are working:
You have a clear ICP definition
that every rep understands and agrees with
Your segmentation is actually done
— not “we segmented by company size” but specific criteria that align with how deals close
Your messaging has been A/B tested
and proven effective before scaling
Your follow-up cadences work
for real (not just theoretical)
You track and measure response rates
by channel and message type
You train new hires properly
before letting them loose
If any part of that feels like a gap, stop immediately and fill it.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen CEOs and founders get angry with their customers.  “How could they do this?” or “Why are they being so unreasonable” or worse, “They don’t know what’s good for them.”
Well … maybe they do.
Maybe your customer is right, at least on some level.
In fact, if you’re doing well enough as an SMB vendor that someone took the time to sign up, pay you — there’s probably something real here.  Something where your product does solve one of his problems better than another solution out there.
So when things go sideways, try these 5 tactics:
First, listen.  Listen more than usual, even if it sounds like they are just venting.  It’s not.  They want you to hear them.  And importantly, they often have a point.  At least, in part.
Second, offer to upgrade their subscription or account.  This will help
de-stress
things.  If nothing else, if you give away a promotion, a discount, etc. — then at least, that won’t be why they leave.
Third, invite him/her to come visit / meet IRL

here
.
Fourth, ask yourself — did we really lose the deal?  Or was it just friction?
Sometimes, no matter how hard you push, you’ll never win back a lost customer.  But sometimes, they just need a little more time.  A little more engagement.   A little bit more love.
Fifth, do whatever it takes to save the renewal.  That’s often 2 years down the road.  So make sure every single customer is happy going into renewal season
.  Because you may lose those deals, too.

The N=1 app is software that’s so specialized, so deeply integrated with your specific workflow and data, that no vendor offers it as a core feature — or if they do, it costs $50K/year plus engineering time to configure. These apps solve real problems but have limited appeal beyond their narrow use case. Think:
Your custom Slack integration for support ticket routing
That one dashboard you built showing revenue by rep AND by month AND by cohort
The Zapier workflow connecting Salesforce contacts to Gong transcripts
Your Google Sheets sheet calculating pipeline velocity by deal stage
These are all powerful tools that make you more efficient. But would anyone else pay for them? Probably not at the price point where you’d need to sell them externally. Third, once you’ve got it working … it really works. And maybe most importantly, fourth, it can’t be easily hacked or kludged into existence by someone without intimate, hands-on experience of how things work in your organization. Within two hours, we had insights on event sponsorship engagement patterns across four years of historical data. This was mission-critical for planning future strategy.
